1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nf6.name: Sicilian Defence: Nimzowitsch Variation
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nf6.background: Named after Aron Nimzowitsch, who pioneered it as one of two provocative variations of the Sicilian Defence; it is also known as the Nimzowitsch–Rubinstein Variation. After 3.e5 Nd5 it resembles Alekhine's Defence.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.e5.strategy: Chases the knight at once and gains space. Black must spend a second move on the same piece, and White's pawn on e5 cramps Black's development, though it also has to be supported against attack in the fight that follows.
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.e5.name: Sicilian Defence: Nimzowitsch Variation, Advance Variation

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Nc3.strategy: A flexible alternative: it defends e4 against the knight and keeps d4 in reserve, steering for a normal Open Sicilian. White gives up the space-gaining but committal e5 advance, so the game is less sharp and Black has an easy time finding a sound set-up.
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Nc3.name: Sicilian Defence: Nimzowitsch Variation, Closed Variation

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.e5 Nd5.strategy: Puts the knight on the best square available: it is central and nothing attacks it yet, and from there it eyes c3, b4 and f4. Black has lost time, but White's advanced e5 pawn now needs support, and the fight for the centre goes on.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Nc3 d6.strategy: Stops e4-e5, which would hit the knight again, and prepares to meet d4 by capturing. Black heads for a standard Open Sicilian with the pawn on d6 and a knight on f6, and avoids the cramped games that the e5 advance gives.
